slides.title: Beyond a good story
slides.subtitle: What 1.45 million Kiva loan descriptions can and cannot tell us about funding speed
lines: Mike Nguyen and Sophia Nguyen, Cultural Blend
Finalists, UNSW Marketing Analytics Hackathon Challenge 2026
slides.visual: Navy ground, yellow accent shape; reuse the sourced Kiva farmer photograph from docs/presentation/poster (credit in notes) in a rounded frame bleeding off the right edge

notes.purpose: Introduce the question and who we are.
notes.script: We are Cultural Blend, one of eight finalist teams in the UNSW Marketing Analytics Hackathon. We analysed 1.45 million Kiva loans to ask whether the way a borrower's story is written is linked to how fast the loan funds. This edition adds two months of follow-up research.
notes.reference: Official results: unsw.edu.au MA-hackathon page (reviewed 2026-10-24). Photo: Kiva farmer photograph, credit Kiva, hosted on kiva.org; provenance in docs/presentation/poster/README.md. It gives context and does not identify a record in the dataset.

slides.title: Text carries forecast information, but no writing tip is proven
slides.subtitle: Summary of the August, October and November evidence

body.heading: Uncertainty first
body.text: 64 of 120 significant terms lost significance once errors were clustered by 48 countries.

body.heading: Most framing links are small
body.text: Family, agency, business and third-person framing are bounded within about ±5% of funding time per extra mention per 100 words. Urgency is unresolved.

body.heading: Text adds forecast information
body.text: Adding text lowered linear forecast error in 5 of 5 years, by 0.26–0.39 days.

takeaways.heading: What it supports
takeaways.text: Use description text as context in research and forecasting.

takeaways.heading: What it does not
takeaways.text: No evidence yet that rewriting a description speeds funding.

takeaways.heading: Next decision
takeaways.text: Validate the text measures, then test one truthful prompt with partners.

notes.purpose: Give the answer before the detail.
notes.script: Three findings. First, the size of the data hid how uncertain many results were: once we accounted for countries, more than half the significant terms fell away. Second, most framing associations are small enough to bound, but urgency is too noisy to judge either way. Third, text does improve forecasts, by about a quarter to two fifths of a day. So text is informative, but we cannot yet say that changing it helps. [Point: Next decision] The next step is measurement and one small pilot.
notes.reference: claims_register.md rows: 64 of 120; equivalence screen; November linear gains.

notes.script: We start with the problem and what the outcome really measures, then our three layers of evidence, then what we found and what we recommend.

slides.title: The description is one of the few listing fields still editable
slides.subtitle: Context: what is fixed and what is editable when a Kiva loan is listed

takeaways.heading: Why the question matters
takeaways.text: Partners and Kiva staff coach descriptions; if framing mattered, coaching would be a cheap lever.

takeaways.heading: What we asked
takeaways.text: Which narrative choices are associated with faster funding, for whom and when?

notes.purpose: Explain why narrative is worth studying.
notes.script: Most of what describes a loan is fixed by the time it is listed. The text is the part someone can still edit, which is why platforms coach it. Our question is whether the way it is written is linked to faster funding.

slides.title: The outcome is platform funding time, not borrower waiting time
slides.subtitle: Descriptive audit of all records; August primary run

key_figures.label: disbursed to the borrower before listing (median 24.2 days earlier)

body.text: 1,453,846 input records; 6 negative durations excluded; 1,637 refunded records included.

takeaways.heading: Who waits
takeaways.text: For most loans the partner has already paid the borrower. Platform time plausibly reflects replenishing partner capital; it is not measured directly.

takeaways.heading: Who is missing
takeaways.text: Only loans that eventually funded are in the data, so we cannot study whether a loan funds at all.

notes.purpose: Set the limits every later claim inherits.
notes.script: Our outcome is the time from listing to full funding. Two facts shape it. Almost all loans were paid out before they were listed, so a faster platform fill plausibly helps the partner replenish capital rather than a waiting borrower. We do not measure that directly. And the data only contain loans that funded.

slides.title: Same-day funding fell from 46.0% to 30.3% and has not recovered
slides.subtitle: Share of loans fully funded within 24 hours by period; descriptive

takeaways.heading: A slower market
takeaways.text: The drop persisted for four years after the disruption.

takeaways.heading: Why it matters here
takeaways.text: Period is a control in every model; narrative effects are judged within periods.

notes.script: Before 2020 almost half of loans funded within a day. That fell to under a third and stayed there. This is descriptive: we do not claim to know why.
notes.reference: notebooks/1_full_dataset_eda.py period trend; counts from association_summary.txt.

slides.title: Three layers of evidence, each answering a different question
slides.subtitle: August primary run, October extension and November benchmark

layers.name: August primary run
layers.question: Which features are associated with speed, and how sure are we?
layers.method: OLS and GLM; HC3 versus country-clustered errors; 2024–2025 chronological holdout

layers.name: October extension
layers.question: Do associations survive richer controls?
layers.method: Country-clustered OLS and LPM with and without a programme-text proxy; BH adjustment

layers.name: November benchmark
layers.question: How much does text add to a structure-only forecast?
layers.method: Matched feature blocks on identical rows; as-of training; five annual windows 2021–2025

exhibit.footer: 8 November: exploratory equivalence screen of the October coefficients

notes.purpose: Explain how the evidence fits together.
notes.script: Each layer answers a different question, so we keep their numbers separate. August asks about associations and their uncertainty. October adds controls. November asks a prediction question: does text improve a forecast built on loan structure alone?

slides.title: Large row counts did not remove country-level uncertainty
slides.subtitle: August primary run: HC3 versus 48-country clustered errors

key_figures.label: significant terms lost significance under country clustering
urgency, duration model, clustered (was p < 0.001 under HC3)

takeaways.heading: Why it happens
takeaways.text: Loans in one country share context, so 1.45 million rows behave like far fewer independent observations.

takeaways.heading: What it does not mean
takeaways.text: Losing significance is not evidence of no effect; the next slide tests that directly.

notes.purpose: Show why we distrust headline significance.
notes.script: With 1.45 million rows almost everything looks significant. When we let errors correlate within each of 48 countries, 64 of the 120 significant terms fell away, including urgency. [Point: What it does not mean] That tells us the evidence is weak, not that the effect is zero.
notes.reference: association_summary.txt sensitivity blocks; recount recorded in claims_register.md.

slides.title: Most framing associations are small; urgency remains unresolved
slides.subtitle: Equivalence screen of October coefficients; exploratory, bound set after the estimates

exhibit.unit: change in log(1 + days) per extra mention per 100 words, 90% interval, expanded specification

takeaways.heading: Small, not just non-significant
takeaways.text: Five framings stay inside ±5% of funding time in both specifications.

takeaways.heading: Too noisy to judge
takeaways.text: Urgency and first-person framing could still be linked to 6–14% faster or slower funding per mention. Each is absent from over 98% of records.

takeaways.heading: Caveat
takeaways.text: The bound was chosen after seeing the estimates; a confirmatory test needs one agreed in advance.

notes.script: The shaded band is a practical bound, about five percent of funding time per extra mention. When a whole interval sits inside the band, we can say the association is small. Most framings do. Urgency and first person do not: their intervals are wide enough to allow sizeable links either way. [Point: Caveat] We chose the bound after seeing the results, so treat this as exploratory. Edit size matters too: one mention in a typical description is a realistic edit, but almost no descriptions contain these words, so the data say little about them.

slides.title: Regional family-framing patterns rest on two countries each
slides.subtitle: August primary run: within-region slopes with country-clustered and heuristic few-cluster intervals

exhibit.unit: change in log(1 + days) per extra family mention per 100 words

takeaways.heading: Two countries is not a pattern
takeaways.text: With two clusters, between-country uncertainty cannot be estimated well; the heuristic intervals cross zero.

takeaways.heading: No regional advice
takeaways.text: These are descriptive patterns, not grounds for country or regional writing rules.

notes.purpose: Prevent over-reading the most striking regional result.
notes.script: Family framing looks linked to faster funding in two regions. But each region is two countries. A t(1) screen, which is a heuristic and not a calibrated test, widens the intervals across zero.

slides.title: Few narrative associations remain after programme controls
slides.subtitle: October extension: country-clustered, BH-adjusted within specification

exhibit.note: Per extra mention per 100 words. BH-adjusted within each specification.

takeaways.heading: Small and mixed
takeaways.text: Third-person framing keeps its size but rises to BH p 0.061; business framing is the one term below BH 0.05.

takeaways.heading: Still associations
takeaways.text: Programme text is an unvalidated proxy; neither result shows what editing would do.

notes.script: Few results remain under richer controls. Third-person framing keeps about the same size, but its adjusted p-value rises just above 0.05. Business framing is the one term that passes after programme controls, with a slightly lower same-day rate. Both are small and observational.

key_figures.label: third-person BH p, expanded to programme-adjusted

slides.title: Adding text lowered forecast error in 5 of 5 years
slides.subtitle: November benchmark: linear model, structure only versus structure plus text, identical evaluation rows

takeaways.heading: Text is informative
takeaways.text: Gains of 0.26–0.39 days on 728,640 evaluation records.

takeaways.heading: Not an editing effect
takeaways.text: Text may encode purpose, place or programme templates, not only persuasion.

notes.script: We trained on earlier years and tested on each of 2021 to 2025, comparing the same model with and without text on the same loans. Text reduced error every year.

slides.title: The gain is modest and depends on the model
slides.subtitle: November benchmark: annual MAE gain with month-resampled 95% intervals

series.name: Linear, adds form, lexicon and TF-IDF

takeaways.heading: Model matters
takeaways.text: The tree model, without TF-IDF, gains at most 0.04 days.

takeaways.heading: Countries matter
takeaways.text: Country resampling includes zero in 4 of 5 linear years. Capping extreme forecasts, an exploratory check, leaves zero in 1 of 5.

takeaways.heading: Metrics disagree
takeaways.text: In 2025 text improved error and calibration but AUC fell from 0.893 to 0.888.

notes.script: The linear gains are consistent month to month, but country resampling is less kind, and the tree model gains little. [Point: Countries matter] Part of that country fragility comes from a few extreme forecasts: when we cap forecasts at the longest training wait, an exploratory check, the country interval excludes zero in 4 of 5 years. Different metrics also move in different directions.
notes.reference: docs/6_matched_text_results.md; reports/loss_alignment_2025/README.md (all five years, capped diagnostic).

slides.title: What the evidence supports, and what it does not
slides.subtitle: Synthesis across all layers

columns.heading: Supported
items: Text adds forecast information in a linear model
Platform funding time is not borrower waiting time for most loans

columns.heading: Not established
items: That editing a description speeds funding
Any country or regional writing rule
Effects of urgency or first-person framing
Performance on loans that never funded

notes.script: On the left, what we can stand behind. On the right, what we cannot claim, however tempting.

slides.title: Three gates before any writing advice
slides.subtitle: Proposed next research for Kiva and participating partners

steps.name: Validate
steps.text: Dual-code a sample of narratives for clarity, specificity, need and agency; freeze definitions.

steps.name: Close data gaps
steps.text: Partner identifiers, all listings including expired ones, original text versions.

steps.name: Pilot
steps.text: One truthful clarity prompt versus control, with a practical threshold and power agreed in advance.

notes.script: Before anyone tells borrowers how to write, three things need to happen, in order.

slides.title: The two-country screen in full
slides.content: Regional slope table with clusters, loans, estimates, normal and t(1) intervals; explain why one- or two-country groups cannot estimate between-country uncertainty.
slides.subtitle: August primary run: within-region family-framing slopes in log(1 + days) per extra mention per 100 words

body.heading: Why two countries are not enough
body.text: A one-country group cannot estimate between-country uncertainty, and two countries estimate it poorly. The t(1) reference keeps the same clustered standard error and widens the interval.

body.heading: What the screen is
body.text: A heuristic sensitivity screen, not a calibrated correction. Passing it would not certify a result, so these patterns stay descriptive.

notes.purpose: Show the regional screen in full.
notes.script: This is the detail behind the regional slide. With two countries per region, the usual interval is too narrow, and the t(1) screen shows how much it could widen.

slides.title: As-of training audit
slides.content: Cohort table from docs/6_matched_text_results.md (pre-cutoff postings completing later, eligible training, evaluation rows per year).
slides.subtitle: November benchmark: training records must have completed before each cutoff
slides.note: Note: The 2024 replay excludes 5,691 training records that a posting-only split would keep. Evaluation windows still select eventual completions.

notes.purpose: Show how training stayed honest about time.
notes.script: A training record only counts if it had finished funding before the cutoff, so the model never learns from outcomes that were not yet known.

slides.title: Primary prediction metrics
slides.content: HistGradientBoosting duration MAE 5.2031 days, R² 0.5420; classifier ROC AUC 0.8997, AP 0.8301, Brier 0.1156; 1,174,953 train, 278,887 holdout; completed loans only.
slides.subtitle: August primary run: chronological holdout, completed loans only
slides.note: Scope: 1,174,953 training and 278,887 holdout loans (2024–2025). Retrospective predictions on completed loans, not deployment estimates.

notes.script: These are the August benchmark scores. They come from a different model and split from the November benchmark, so the two sets of numbers should not be compared directly.

slides.title: Exploratory story themes
slides.content: NMF themes from the 20,000-loan exploratory sample, labelled as such; not full-data evidence.
slides.subtitle: Exploratory NMF themes from a 20,000-loan sample; descriptive, not full-data evidence

key_figures.label: mean funding time, slowest theme (group solar and farm plots)

body.heading: What the themes show
body.text: 8 themes, including sanitation, clean water, livestock, smallholder farming and retail. They track loan purpose as much as writing style.

body.heading: How to read them
body.text: Means are unadjusted and come from a sample, so the gap is context, not a tested effect of story content.

notes.script: Topic modelling gave coherent themes, but on a 20,000-loan sample and without adjustment. Topics mostly describe what the loan is for, so they are context rather than evidence about writing.
